title: Let nothing disturb thee
hook: a short poem found in her breviary: all things pass, God does not change, God alone suffices

segments.voice: Yesterday, spiritual marriage: Martha and Mary together at the center of the castle. Today, our last day with Teresa, and nine short lines.

A note folded in a wallet. A line taped inside a cabinet. A verse on a sticky note on the bathroom mirror. Something short enough to read with a toothbrush in your mouth, and strong enough to get through a day. Teresa of Ávila had one too. Tradition says that after she died, her sisters found it tucked in her breviary, the prayer book she carried every day. Nine lines. People still copy them out.
screen: `A SCRAP OF PAPER, KEPT CLOSE.` → `TUCKED IN HER PRAYER BOOK.` → `NINE LINES.`

segments.voice: In Teresa's Spanish, it begins: "Nada te turbe, nada te espante." Let nothing disturb you, nothing frighten you. The old English version begins, let nothing disturb thee. First, the worry. Teresa did not live a quiet life: lawsuits, sickness, travel on broken roads, officials who tried to shut down her convents. These lines aren't a greeting card. They read like what a hard-pressed woman told herself. Second, what passes. Everything passes, the next lines say. God does not change. Your worry, your triumph, your bad week, the officials who hate you: all of it passes. Third, patience. Then: patience obtains everything. Not quick results. The steady waiting she learned over a lifetime of prayer. Fourth, enough. The ending is the part people carve on walls and stitch on cushions: whoever has God lacks nothing. And the last three words in Spanish: "Sólo Dios basta." God alone is enough. That doesn't mean Teresa didn't need friends, food or sleep. She loved her friends fiercely and wrote to them constantly. It means that underneath everything, when all of it shakes, there is a floor. For Teresa, that floor had a name.
screen: `WRITTEN FROM A HARD LIFE.` · `ALL THINGS PASS. GOD DOES NOT.` · `PATIENCE OBTAINS EVERYTHING.` · `WHOEVER HAS GOD LACKS NOTHING.` · then, large: `SÓLO DIOS BASTA.`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper or a sticky note, write the first line, let nothing disturb thee, or the last, God alone is enough. Hold it, think of one thing that's disturbing you right now, and read the line to it. If you pray, pray Teresa's lines as she did; if you don't, let the words steady you.
Breviary. The prayer book Teresa carried every day, where her sisters found her nine lines after she died, including: God alone is enough. Today's word.
Your line: god alone is enough. Teresa's castle, done. Tomorrow, John of the Cross, the friend she loved and teased.

howItsDone: Many Catholics keep Teresa's Nada te turbe on a prayer card or say it in hard moments, and the Taizé community sings it as a short, repeated chant.

notes: The Spanish lines ('Nada te turbe, / nada te espante', 'Sólo Dios basta') are quoted from the original; confirm spelling and accents. Middle lines (todo se pasa, Dios no se muda, la paciencia todo lo alcanza, quien a Dios tiene nada le falta) are rendered in English paraphrase.
The breviary discovery is tradition; stated as 'tradition says'.
Longfellow's translation ('Let nothing disturb thee…') is 19th-century and public domain but not on the validator's list, so it isn't quoted beyond the index title.
Teresa died in October 1582 at Alba de Tormes; confirm.
